content.thinking:
Since there's no actual evidence to draw from, I need to write the postmortem honestly: root cause unknown, no metrics were actually read, and duration should be described as unknown rather than inventing a figure. I'll avoid restating any numbers as if computed and instead describe things qualitatively—the issue appears still unresolved as of the last check, with duration genuinely unclear.

I should also list my assumptions explicitly: that the alert is genuine, that its timestamp marks the actual onset, that the service stayed impaired throughout, and that the absence of flag changes in provider history only rules out feature-flag triggers, not other config changes.

assumptions: The alert is assumed to reflect a real fault; this was not independently confirmed, as no metrics were read back.
The alert timestamp is used as the start of impact because no onset could be measured; actual onset may have been earlier.
The service is assumed to have remained impaired through the end of the available data, since no recovery was observed; this is not the same as confirming it was still broken.

The flag provider reported no recent changes, which was taken to mean a feature-flag change is unlikely to be the trigger; this covers flags only and does not rule out deploys, configuration, dependencies, or infrastructure.
Customer impact is assumed to be non-zero because an error-rate alert fired, but its scale and the number of affected users are unknown.
input.executive_summary:
An automated alert reported an elevated rate of failed requests on one of our services. The automated responder picked the incident up, tried to pull the service's recent minute-by-minute metrics, and got nothing back, so it could not confirm what was failing, how many requests or customers were affected, or how bad it was. With no evidence to work from, it handed the incident to a human on-call team shortly after the alert fired.

Because the metrics could not be read, the duration and the customer impact of this incident are unknown. What can be said is that the service had not been observed recovering by the end of the data that was available, so the problem lasted at least from the moment the alert fired and possibly longer; any figure in the incident record describing elapsed time is a floor, not a measurement. The time the automated responder held the incident before escalating describes how quickly it handed off, not how long customers were affected.

No remediation was performed by the automated responder, and no cause was identified. Follow-up should start with why metrics for this window were unavailable, since that gap - not the error rate itself - is what prevented any assessment of impact.
input.root_cause: Not determined. An alert fired for a high error rate on io-shop, but the investigation retrieved no per-minute metrics for the incident window and the flag provider showed no recent changes, so no candidate cause could be evidenced or ruled out; the incident was escalated to humans for insufficient evidence rather than diagnosed.
